In twenty twenty-two, America made a bet: if China can't get the best chips, it can't build the best AI.

China answered with metals the whole world needs. Smugglers answered with fake labels. And then a small Chinese start-up wiped almost six hundred billion dollars off one American company, in a single day.
Let's follow the fight, move by move.
Move one. The seventh of October, twenty twenty-two. Washington.
The US Commerce Department announced new rules. Nvidia's most powerful AI chips could no longer be sold to China. Neither could the tools to make advanced chips.
Why chips? Why not ban the AI itself?
Because AI is trained on chips. Thousands of them, running for weeks. Without the best chips, building the best models gets slower and far more expensive.
And Washington said it was about national security, including military uses.
It built a version just for China: the A eight hundred and the H eight hundred. Same brains, slower links between the chips.
A year later, the rules tightened. Those chips were banned too, and the controls spread to more than forty countries.
So Nvidia built another China chip, the H twenty. In April twenty twenty-five, that one needed a licence too. Nvidia booked a four-and-a-half-billion-dollar charge.
Not quite. In August twenty twenty-five, Washington allowed H twenty sales, in exchange for fifteen percent of the revenue.
Then Beijing told its own companies not to buy them. Nvidia sold no H twenties to China that quarter.
In December, Washington went further: the more powerful H two hundred could go to approved Chinese buyers, with twenty-five percent for the US government.
From a ban... to a tax?
Almost. But China barely let them in, and by November twenty twenty-six, Nvidia had stopped shipping them.
And a ban creates something else too: a black market.
Move two. When something valuable is banned, someone tries to smuggle it.
In a case US prosecutors called Operation Gatekeeper, a businessman and his company exported at least one hundred and sixty million dollars of Nvidia's top chips.
How did they get past customs?
They relabelled the chips with a fake brand name, and declared them as ordinary computer parts. In October twenty twenty-five, they pleaded guilty.
In another case, four people were charged with routing chips through Malaysia and Thailand. Investigators intercepted supercomputers packed with Nvidia chips on the way.
In March twenty twenty-six, a co-founder of Supermicro, a big American server maker, was arrested.

Prosecutors allege two and a half billion dollars of servers went to a South-East Asian company, and about five hundred million dollars' worth was sent on to China, with dummy servers to fool inspectors.
One co-defendant has pleaded guilty. The co-founder has pleaded not guilty, and his trial is set for twenty twenty-seven.
But China wasn't only trying to get around the rules. It was getting ready to hit back.
Move three. July twenty twenty-three. Beijing.
China announced export licences for two metals most people have never heard of: gallium and germanium.
Because China makes ninety-nine percent of the world's primary gallium.
Gallium nitride is the material in powerful modern radar, like the radars of air-defence systems. It's also in LED lights and power chips.
Germanium carries light through fibre-optic cables, and sharpens night-vision lenses.
In December twenty twenty-four, one day after a new US chip package, China banned exports of both metals to America outright.
Prices went wild. In Europe, gallium more than doubled. Germanium hit about five thousand dollars a kilo, around five times its early twenty twenty-three price.
After Trump and Xi met in South Korea, the ban on America was paused... for now.
But metals were only a warning shot. The real weapon was something smaller.
Far stronger. Rare-earth magnets sit inside electric motors, cars, drones and wind turbines.
China mines about sixty percent of these rare earths, refines about ninety percent, and makes ninety-four percent of the magnets.
The biggest source is here: Bayan Obo, in Inner Mongolia, the world's largest rare-earth mine.
In April twenty twenty-five, China put seven rare earths, and magnets containing them, under export licences.
In May, its magnet exports fell seventy-four percent in a single month. Exports to America fell ninety-three percent.
Within weeks, Ford halted its Chicago factory for about a week. In Europe, parts suppliers shut production lines.
In October, China added five more rare earths, plus a rule reaching foreign factories: products with even a small share of Chinese rare earths would need a Chinese licence.
That's why, at the end of October twenty twenty-five, Trump and Xi agreed a truce, and the October rules were paused.

The West is racing to catch up. The Pentagon bought into a rare-earth mine in California and promised it a minimum price. In Malaysia, Lynas became the first to produce heavy rare earths outside China.
But ninety-four percent of the magnets still come from one country.
So America had the chips, and China had the metals. Then the fight moved somewhere nobody expected: an app store.
Move five. Hangzhou. A start-up called DeepSeek, spun out of a Chinese hedge fund.
On the twentieth of January twenty twenty-five, it released a free AI model, R1, which it said could rival OpenAI's best reasoning model.
Its base model was trained on H eight hundreds, the slower chips Nvidia had made for China, which were legal to buy until late twenty twenty-three.
DeepSeek said the final training run cost about five point six million dollars in rented computer time.
Analysts say the real total, with all the research and hardware, was far higher.
But people heard the cheap number?
Within a week, DeepSeek's app was number one on America's App Store, ahead of ChatGPT.
And on the twenty-seventh of January, investors panicked. If AI could be built this cheaply, who would need so many Nvidia chips?
Nvidia's stock fell seventeen percent. About five hundred and ninety billion dollars of value, gone in one day: the biggest one-day loss in US stock market history.
So did the chip bans fail?
Most experts say they leaked rather than failed: chips bought before the rules, and chips that were legal for a while.
And Nvidia recovered. Nine months later, it became the first company ever worth five trillion dollars.
But in April twenty twenty-six, DeepSeek released a new model made to run on Chinese Huawei chips.
So look at the scoreboard. America banned the chips. Smugglers found new routes. China cut off the metals. Its magnets stopped car factories. And a free app shook Wall Street.
Five moves. And nobody has won yet.
Because both sides still need the same thing: chips printed by one Dutch machine, on one island.
